description: Hooks. A 'plan-' case gives a 'manifest' (or, with none, an overlay's 'files' by path and text, its manifest read from them) and the consumer's 'facts': os, files, interpreters (absent, all five), identity, scope ('overlay', the default, 'user' or 'project'), digest (the overlay's; absent, unknown), tree (for a project, every file of the directory holding its configuration, by path and text, whose tree digest is the digest), allowed (the one digest at which the user allowed its hooks), fires (the events the consumer can fire on this harness; absent, every one), partial (those it fires for only some occurrences) and limits ('timeout', the consumer's bound on a run, in seconds); 'expect' gives each hook in event order (event, path and interpreter, or null for a hook.<ext> none of which can run here; whether it 'runs' here; match, sets, timeout after the bound, on_failure, and the payload's keys), whether they are 'on', whether the overlay 'activates', the interpreters a probe 'needs', the 'reports' ([id, subject]) and 'non_defaults' ([id, subject]), and the manifest's 'issues' (pointers). A 'payload-' case gives an 'event' and what the consumer knows ('known'); 'expect' is the payload. An 'output-' case gives an 'event', one 'run' ('stdout', or 'stdout_base64', or 'stdout_parts' as [text, times]; 'exit', default 0; 'timed_out'; 'not_run'; 'payload_size'; 'sets', the variables its entry declares) and optional 'limits' ('max_output', 'max_payload'); 'expect' is the 'output' that applies, or the cause it 'failed' with. An 'event-' case gives an 'event', its 'runs' in order (each with its 'source', 'match' (absent: none), 'on_failure', default 'report', and the 'seconds' it took), the tool 'kind' of a 'pre-tool' call (absent: one no run's match is checked against), what the consumer 'applies' on this harness ('context', 'env', 'block', 'deny', 'ask', 'allow', 'refuse'; absent, all the event takes, and refuse), 'limits' (also 'event_timeout') and 'os'; 'expect' gives the sources that 'ran', the 'decision' ('block', 'deny', 'ask', 'allow', 'refuse' or null), the source it was 'by' and the hook's own 'reason' (null for a refusal by failure), the 'context' as [source, text], the 'env' (null unsets), the 'reports' and the 'non_defaults'. A 'match-' case gives an 'event', a 'match' (or null) and the reason or tool kind ('value'); 'expect' says whether the hook 'runs'. A 'pre-tool' 'event-' case may give the call's 'input' (an object), and 'expect' then also gives what each hook 'seen' as [source, input] and the 'input' the call runs with (null: the one it was given). An 'event-' case may give 'context_used', the bytes the session's context already holds, and 'limits' may give 'context_bytes' (default 1 MiB). An 'order-' case gives 'overlays', 'requested', the overlays that 'has' a hook for the event and the 'scopes' (user, project) that have one; 'expect' is the 'order' of [scope, source] pairs. A 'process-' case gives a 'process' ('setup', 'server', 'command' or 'env-script') and the same 'overlays', 'requested', 'files', 'facts' and 'identity' as an 'environment-' case; 'expect' is the 'env' that process runs with: the session's, and for an env script the environment as it stands when it runs. An 'environment-' case gives an 'event', 'overlays', 'requested', optional 'files' (an overlay's env file texts), the compose 'facts' (os, base_env, roots, states, pre_env, grants, secrets, and 'earlier': the 'env' outputs earlier hooks of the event set, in run order, null unsetting) and the hook, an 'identity' or a 'scope' of user or project; 'expect' is the 'env' it runs with.

cases.description: hook.py and no manifest: the events without content, off until the user allows the overlay's hooks at its digest.
Allowed at this digest: each event is reported as the non_default hook.
Allowed at another digest: an update turns them off until allowed again.
A digest compares without regard to case.
One allowance per identity: going back to a digest the user allowed before needs a new yes.
A consumer that has not computed the overlay's digest allows nothing.
The user's own configuration needs no allowance.
A project's configuration arrives with a checkout: off until allowed.
Allowed at the digest of every file in the directory that holds its configuration.
A file added beside an allowed script (a json.py its import would load) changes the digest: off until allowed again.
A guard that is off would fail open, so an overlay with one is not activated until the user allows its hooks.
An event the consumer fires for only some occurrences (the calls the harness asks about) is reported as partial.
A table's sets lists the variables its env output may set.
prompt, pre-tool and post-tool carry the user's words or a tool's input: hook.<ext> never gets them by default.
A table with no run gives a content event to hook.<ext>; its payload lists what it learns.
A declared event takes the default entry's place, so hook.py does not also run at session-start; other events keep hook.py.
false runs nothing for that event, hook.<ext> included.
[defaults] hooks = false: hook.py has no default events, and means nothing.
With the default off, the declared events still run hook.<ext>.
A table's match, timeout and on_failure are kept; timeout defaults to 30.
The consumer's setting bounds every run: a longer timeout is cut to it, a shorter one kept.
hook.<ext> chosen by runtime as env.<ext> is: with no Python, hook.ps1 on Windows.
And hook.sh elsewhere: hook.ps1 applies only on Windows.
With every interpreter, .py comes first.
Only hook.ps1, on Linux: no default event runs, and the file is reported as script-not-run.
A declared guard whose hook.<ext> cannot run here stays listed, so firing it fails and refuses: it fails closed.
A declared script whose interpreter the consumer lacks: listed, not runnable, and needed, so a probe passes this target over.
hook.cfg, Hook.py, hooks/hook.py and a hook.py under an excluded directory are no hook.<ext>.
Nothing to run: nothing is reported.
Events the consumer cannot fire on this harness are reported, each by name, never skipped silently.
A consumer that fires no hook on this harness reports every one.
hooks under a harness hint is that harness's data: it adds no hook.
In OVERLAY.md the front matter holds hooks, as overlay.cfg would.

files.OVERLAY.md:
---
name: shell-guard
hooks:
  pre-tool:
    match: [execute]
    on_failure: refuse
  turn-end: false
---
Force pushes are refused.

cases.description: And in a #!toml front matter.

files.OVERLAY.md:
---
#!toml
[hooks]
pre-tool = { match = ["execute"], on_failure = "refuse" }
turn-end = false
---
Force pushes are refused.

cases.description: And in overlay.cfg.
What a pre-env hook is told, of everything the consumer knows: its event's keys and nothing else.
What a session-start hook is told, of everything the consumer knows: its event's keys and nothing else.
What a session-end hook is told, of everything the consumer knows: its event's keys and nothing else.
What a prompt hook is told, of everything the consumer knows: its event's keys and nothing else.
What a turn-end hook is told, of everything the consumer knows: its event's keys and nothing else.
What a cd hook is told, of everything the consumer knows: its event's keys and nothing else.
What a pre-compact hook is told, of everything the consumer knows: its event's keys and nothing else.
What a pre-tool hook is told, of everything the consumer knows: its event's keys and nothing else.
What a post-tool hook is told, of everything the consumer knows: its event's keys and nothing else.
A key the consumer does not know is absent, never null.
No output: nothing to apply.
Only white space is no output.
Context, on an event that takes it.
One object over several lines.
An empty context is kept as written and adds nothing.
Only pre-env reads one object per line; anywhere else two objects are not one.
An array is no output.
Plain text is no output: a hook's words reach the agent only as context.
Not UTF-8.
The manifest's JSON rules: a duplicate key is refused.
And NaN.
Another key is a failure: additionalContext is Claude Code's, not a hook's.
A harness's own vocabulary means nothing from a hook, and is not passed on: the key is another.
allow is pre-tool's: the consumer answers the harness's approval as approved.
An allow takes a reason and context.
A decision value no event has is an output failure.
allow is pre-tool's; a prompt is blocked.
session-start takes no decision, allow included.
Any decision that is not the event's own is an output failure.
Continuing is not a decision a hook can make.
An empty decision.
A decision that is not a string.
Decisions match exactly: Deny is not deny.
session-start takes no decision.
deny is pre-tool's; a prompt is blocked.
block is not pre-tool's; a call is denied.
updatedInput is Claude Code's name for it, another key here: the whole output fails.
An allow may carry the call it approves, as rewritten.
A rewritten input comes only with an allow.
An input with no decision is no approval, and fails.
The input is an object, as a call's arguments are.
post-tool takes no input.
A deny and its reason.
A reason is optional.
ask, with context.
A prompt blocked.

output.reason: The prompt names a production host.

cases.description: A compaction blocked.
A reason without a decision.
A reason is text.
No zero byte in context.
cd takes variables only: its context would not reach the model.
turn-end takes no output.
Nor does session-end.
Variables, null unsetting one.
prompt takes variables where the consumer can.
And pre-tool, for an execute call.
A variable the entry does not list in sets is a failure: what a hook may set is in the manifest.
With no sets, no variable.
Two names equal without regard to ASCII case, which Windows holds as one.
An empty env sets nothing, and needs no sets.
A terminal escape in a reason could repaint the approval it is shown beside.
Nor a bidirectional override.
Nor a C1 control in context.
Nor a bidirectional isolate.
Tabs, line feeds and carriage returns are text.
A reason is at most 1024 code points.
1024 is allowed, counted in code points.
post-tool takes no variables.
Not even one a consumer was told the hook sets: the event takes none.
Nor turn-end.
Nor pre-compact.
No reserved variable: another overlay's root.
Nor AOS_*, in any case.
A variable name.
A value is a string or null.
Without a zero byte.
env is a mapping.
pre-env's output is an env script's: one object.
Or one object per line.
Or one object over several lines.
pre-env takes only variables: context and decision are variable names there.
pre-env cannot set a reserved variable either.
pre-env values are strings, not tables.
A non-zero exit fails the run, whatever it printed.
Exit status 2 is a failure, not a block: a hook blocks by its output.
Stopped at its time.
Output past the default bound, 64 KiB.
Output exactly at the bound is read.
The bound is a setting.
A payload past its bound: the hook is not run, which is a failure.
That bound is a setting too.
Its interpreter could not start it.
Causes in a fixed order: a timeout before its output's size.
Size before the exit status.
No hook: nothing applies.
Context from each hook, in run order, each marked with its overlay; an empty one adds nothing.
A deny ends the event: the hooks after it do not run, and nothing else of the event applies.
A later deny is tighter than an ask.
ask lets the later hooks run, and their context applies.
The first ask is the one reported.
On a harness that cannot ask, ask is applied as deny, which is tighter, and reported.
A blocked prompt: context from before the block does not apply, since the prompt is not sent.
A failure is reported and the event goes on as if that hook had output nothing.
on_failure = refuse: a guard that times out denies the call.
A prompt guard that fails blocks the prompt.
A guard whose interpreter cannot start fails closed.
Where the consumer cannot refuse a session on this harness, the refusal is reported and the event goes on.
Where it can, the session is refused.
A compaction guard that fails blocks the compaction.
An allow alone: the call is approved, by the hook that said so.
An allow lets later hooks run, and their context applies; the first allow is the one reported.
A deny beats an earlier allow and ends the event.
A deny ends the event: a later allow never runs.
An ask beats a later allow; the reason is the ask's.
An ask beats an earlier allow.
Where the consumer cannot answer an allow on this harness, it is reported, never dropped, and the call goes as if no hook allowed.
A decision that is no value of the event is an output failure and nothing of it applies; the next hook runs.
A hook that fails with on_failure refuse denies even after an allow.
A call of kind other runs a hook scoped to read, but its allow does not count and nor does the input it carries: the call is left to the user, and the allow is reported.
A hook with no match may allow a call of kind other, with its input.
A hook whose match names other may allow a call of kind other.
A hook scoped to read still runs on a call of kind other, and its deny counts.
An allow with an input: the call is approved as rewritten.
A later hook is given the rewritten input, and rewrites it again; the call runs with the last.
A deny after a rewrite wins: the call does not run, and nothing is rewritten.
An ask after a rewrite wins: the user is asked about the call as the harness gave it, and the rewrite is reported, never dropped silently.
An ask before a rewrite wins as well.
Where the consumer cannot apply a rewritten input, the allow is not applied either, and that is reported.
A guard whose decision is no value of the event fails closed: the call is denied.
Variables apply in run order; a later hook replaces, or unsets, an earlier one's.
On Windows a later hook's Path sets the PATH an earlier one set, keeping its spelling.
Elsewhere they are two variables.
A variable a deny dropped is not reported: it was never set.
The event has a bound of its own: a hook that would start after it has passed fails, and a guard among them refuses.
That bound is a setting.
A sensitive variable is reported as env-sensitive, a harness's configuration directory included.
On a harness where the consumer cannot set variables, they are reported as not applied; the context still applies.
Context the consumer cannot add is reported, never dropped silently.
A block the consumer cannot apply is reported; the rest of that hook's output applies.
A denied call runs no command, so the variables of its event do not apply.
pre-env: variables from each hook, a failure reported.
A pre-env guard that fails stops the session before the harness starts.
turn-end takes no decision: a hook cannot keep the agent working.
session-end takes no output: anything is a failure, reported.
The output bound is a setting, for every hook of the event.
A tool kind in match runs the hook.
Another kind does not.
A tool the consumer could not place (other) runs every pre-tool hook, so no tool slips past a guard by its kind.
And every post-tool hook.
No match: every call.
A session reason in match.
Another reason does not; other is no reason.
A part of context past the bound is not added, whole and never cut, and reported; a later part that fits still is.
A part that reaches the bound exactly fits; the next byte does not.
The bound counts the bytes of the UTF-8 text, not its characters.
What the session already holds counts: with 8 of 10 bytes used, three more do not fit and two do.
The default bound is 1 MiB.
Context of a run that failed was never added, so it does not count.
Where the consumer cannot add context at all, that is the report, once per part, bound or not.
Overlays, then the user's own, then the project's: the user's deny ends the event before the project's hook runs.
Context is added in that run order, each part marked with where it came from.
A later hook's variable replaces an earlier one's: the project's replaces the user's, which replaced an overlay's.
Overlays in composition order: ascending priority.
Equal priorities by name.
An overlay with no hook for the event is not in the order.
A required overlay is active though not asked for, and runs its hook in its place.
The user's own hooks, then the project's, after every overlay's.
That order is the same however the consumer lists the scopes.
An overlay named user is an overlay, in its composition place.
A project's hook alone.
Both scopes, no overlay with a hook.
An overlay's hook gets the session's environment: every overlay's declarations, each with the value it was substituted to in the session's order.
The first overlay in composition order sees a later overlay's declarations too: they are the session's.
A secret one overlay was granted is in the session's environment, so another overlay's hook has it.
The overlay it was granted to has it as well.
A second overlay's hook reads the variable the first overlay declared, as the agent does.
What earlier hooks of the event set is in the environment of a later one, a null unsetting; later values replace earlier ones.
A pre-env hook sees what earlier pre-env hooks set, in composition order, and not its own or a later one's: low runs first and sees nothing.
Overlays stack: the later overlay's value reads the earlier one's (LEVEL, SHARED) and sits on top, so the earlier overlay's own hook sees the finished stack.
AOS_OVERLAY_ROOT, AOS_OVERLAY_NAME and AOS_OVERLAY_STATE, as a step has them, and AOS_HOOK_EVENT; every overlay's root and state variable is set in each overlay's process.
An overlay with no state directory has no AOS_OVERLAY_STATE.
Every overlay's pre-env output is in the session's environment, so a hook sees another's.
A pre-env hook sees the base, every root and state variable and the pre-env output of overlays before it in composition order, and no declaration: high runs after low.
The user's own hook gets the session's environment and AOS_HOOK_EVENT, and no AOS_OVERLAY_*.
So does a project's.
Every overlay's path addition is in the session's value, the later overlay's first.
An env file's lines are its overlay's own declarations too.
On Windows a name set under another case keeps the spelling the base has.
An overlay's setup gets the session's environment: another overlay's declarations too.
So does an MCP server it starts.
So does a command it exposes.
An env script gets the environment as it stands when it runs: an earlier overlay's declarations and its own, not a later overlay's.
The first overlay's env script does not see a later overlay's declarations.
An env script of the later overlay gets the stack as it stands at its step: the earlier overlay's values and its own declarations over them.
